chapterName: Empire: Augustus and the Principate (27 BC-AD 14)

questions.question: Which Augustan monument near the Field of Mars has carved panels of priests and Roman families in procession?
options: The Temple of Mars the Avenger
questions.explanation: The Altar of Peace (Ara Pacis) rose near the Field of Mars, a riverside district north of the old centre. Its panels show priests, guards and families in procession.
questions.sourceQuote: Near the Field of Mars, a riverside district north of the old centre, rose the Altar of Peace (*Ara Pacis*), its carved panels showing priests, guards and Roman families in procession.

questions.question: How many Roman legions were led into the trap in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9?
questions.explanation: The governor was persuaded to march three legions home by an unfamiliar route. Between 15,000 and 20,000 Romans died.
questions.sourceQuote: He fed the governor false reports of a revolt and persuaded him to march three legions home by an unfamiliar route.

questions.question: Who was the loyal friend and gifted commander who won Octavian's battles for him?
questions.explanation: Octavian was no great general, but he had Agrippa. In 36 BC Agrippa destroyed the fleet of a renegade admiral whose blockades had starved Italy.
questions.sourceQuote: Octavian was no great general, but he had Agrippa, his loyal friend and gifted commander.

questions.question: What name was given to the long era of calm that began under Augustus?
questions.explanation: The Roman Peace, or Pax Romana, lasted with interruptions for about two centuries, as major wars inside the empire largely ceased.
questions.sourceQuote: This era of calm became known as the Roman Peace (*Pax Romana*), and it lasted, with interruptions, for about two centuries.

questions.question: To which river did Augustus's armies push Rome's frontier?
questions.explanation: His armies completed the conquest of Spain, took the Alps and pushed the frontier to the Danube.
questions.sourceQuote: His armies completed the conquest of Spain, took the Alps and pushed Rome's frontier to the Danube river.

questions.question: In what year was the decisive Battle of Actium fought?
questions.explanation: Actium was fought on 2 September 31 BC in a bay on the western coast of Greece. Agrippa's fleet won the day.
questions.sourceQuote: The decisive clash came on 2 September 31 BC at Actium, a bay on the western coast of Greece.

questions.question: What were Augustus's last words, as reported?
questions.explanation: His reported last words were "Acta est fabula, plaudite". He died at Nola, near Naples, in AD 14.
questions.sourceQuote: His last words were reportedly "The play is over; applaud" (*Acta est fabula, plaudite*).

questions.question: Which man did Augustus adopt in AD 4 and raise to powers equal to his own by AD 13?
questions.explanation: Tiberius, his wife's elder son from her first marriage, was a hard-working general with victories in Germany and the Balkans.
questions.sourceQuote: In AD 4 Augustus adopted him, and by AD 13 Tiberius held powers equal to his own.

questions.question: How was the future Augustus related to Julius Caesar by birth?
questions.explanation: His great advantage was his mother, a niece of Julius Caesar. Caesar's will later named him main heir and adopted son.
questions.sourceQuote: His great advantage was his mother, a niece of Julius Caesar, the general who had made himself master of Rome.

questions.question: What does the name "Augustus", granted by the Senate in 27 BC, mean?
questions.explanation: Augustus means "the revered". The name carried a religious glow, hinting that he stood close to the gods.
questions.sourceQuote: The same day the Senate gave him a new name: Augustus (*augustus*), meaning "the revered".
